Dancing With the Stars pro Jenna Johnson confirmed to E! News that a “little accident” such as a broken nose can’t stop her and Harry Shum Jr. as they look ahead to the semifinals.

Jenna Johnson is putting her best nose, er, foot forward.

Despite taking an accidental hit to the face the day before the Dancing With the Stars quarterfinals on Nov. 10, Johnson confirmed she isn’t going to let the broken bone affect her and Harry Shum Jr.’s performances.

“It's so funny, these little accidents always happen,” she exclusively told E! News following the show’s Grammys night. “Dance is a physical contact sport, and I want to always represent dancers as athletes. Just like any other professional athlete would get a little dinged up here or there, they would still go compete.”

“They kept asking me,” she added, like, ‘Do you want someone to dance for you?’ And I was like, ‘No, I love this dance. I've loved dancing this week with Harry. Like, no one is keeping me off the freaking dance floor.’”

And a good thing, too, since their salsa to “Die With a Smile” earned an impressive 29 out of a possible 30 points.

Plus, it helped that the people in Johnson’s life all have a nose for how to best carry her through the performance, despite the injury.

“I've been so supported,” the 32-year-old said. “So, I have to thank all the teams that were there for me last night. But yeah, it's just part of the show.”

Shum, however, wasn’t ready for his partner to brush off her accomplishment.

“It also speaks to you,” the Grey’s Anatomy star emphasized. “Dancers don't get enough credit for how much pain they go through—their feet, injuries in their knees, their back, and like your nose.”

He added, “And to say like, ‘Nope, I'm going to keep going,’ because you love to perform. But also, you work so hard for something and you said, ‘No, I'm not going to let this stop me if it doesn't need to.’”

And stop her it won’t, with the two ready to lead each other on a merry dance all the way through the semifinals.

“Jenna always has a strategy,” Shum emphasized, “and I follow whatever she has in store.”

Meanwhile, Johnson noted it truly takes two to tango.

“You are so smart when it comes to things,” she added. “I love that leading up to this moment, I think we were very thoughtful about what we wanted to do in the semifinals if we had the opportunity to be here. And I'm super excited.”

#829. On this day in space! Nov. 8, 2005: Europe launches Venus Express, its first mission to Venus

Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation at Venus, but it persevered for nine years.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. The spacecraft was called Venus Express.

Venus is a hothouse planet, one where the atmospheric pressure can easily crush an unprotected spacecraft. Even from orbit, Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation. But the spacecraft lasted for more than nine years.

During that time, Venus Express saw a weird vortex swirling around Venus's south pole. It also saw possible signs of active volcanoes. Venus Express also discovered that the planet generates its own auroras. These auroras happen when particles from the sun hit charged particles in the atmosphere.

Late in the Venus Express mission, controllers told the spacecraft to dip down into Venus's clouds — even though the spacecraft wasn't designed to do this. It performed well, but eventually it stopped listening to commands. The spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere in January 2015.

Venus Express established ESA as the third world organization to successfully send a probe to study Venus, following the United States and Soviet Union. (Japan's JAXA became the fourth five years later.)

"By studying Venus, scientists learn how Earth-like planets change over time," reads a summary of the planet's exploration prepared by The Planetary Society. "Orbital studies [like Venus Express] hint that Venus may have hosted habitable oceans before becoming inhospitable."

"By studying Venus, we can learn how Earth-like planets evolve and what shapes planets throughout the galaxy into temperate, lush worlds instead of sweltering hothouses. Venus also helps scientists model Earth’s climate, and may serve as a cautionary tale on how dramatically a planet’s climate can change," wrote the Society.

ESA returned to Venus in 2018 when BepiColombo, its joint mission with JAXA, used the planet's gravity to redirect its path toward the planet Mercury.

Scotland will be without captain Caroline Weir for the World Cup play-off final with Sweden following a setback in her recovery from a muscle injury.

The influential midfielder pulled up in the warm-up before the win over Czech Republic in Paisley a month ago and has not played for Lyon since.

Aston Villa forward Mia McAulay is also missing after a recent calf problem, with Beth Lumsden of Newcastle and Ipswich striker Eilidh Adams added to the squad.

"Of course we're disappointed for Caroline," said head coach Melissa Andreatta. "She's our captain and she has spoken about how much she loves this team.

"But for us, it's all about the players that we have. Our focus is on working together and doing whatever it takes to be on the right side of the result."

Sweden visit Paisley for the first leg on 1 December, with the return game in Stockholm on 5 December.

Andreatta on Weir missing out on play-off final

BBC Scotland will broadcast the opening game while the action in Sweden will be shown by BBC ALBA.

Victory could secure Scotland's spot at Brazil 2027, although there remains the possibility of an intercontinental play-off in February for Europe's lowest ranked play-off final winner.

Sweden have been at every World Cup since the inaugural tournament in 1991 and finished third at the last two editions.

"We don't fear anybody," added Andreatta.

"We have a squad full of quality and we have shown our character and what we are all about.

#827. Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch

Imagine receiving a single treatment that could keep your cholesterol under control for decades, potentially eliminating the need for daily medication. Advances in gene editing are bringing that possibility closer to reality. But scientists say the same technology that could revolutionize medicine also raises difficult questions about safety, permanent genetic changes, and unintended consequences.

Gene therapy is already being used to treat certain serious illnesses. These treatments can introduce working copies of genes, silence harmful genetic activity, or make changes directly to DNA. Unlike conventional medications that must be taken repeatedly, some genetic treatments are designed to work after just one administration.

More than 6,000 rare genetic disorders have been identified, although only a small proportion currently have targets that can be treated. Gene therapies have already achieved important successes against conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy and sickle cell disease.

Now, researchers are exploring whether similar approaches could help prevent or manage far more widespread health problems, including high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes.

That raises a fundamental question: Just because scientists can permanently change a person's genetic activity, does that mean they should?

In a perspective published in JAMA Internal Medicine, University of Michigan Health Frankel Cardiovascular Center cardiologists Eric D. Smith, M.D., and Venkatesh L. Murthy, M.D., Ph.D., outline how doctors and researchers should weigh the potential benefits of genomic therapies against their risks.

The two gene therapy researchers explain why these treatments are so promising, what makes them different from conventional medicines, and what must happen before they can be safely offered to millions of people.

Why One-Time Gene Therapy Is Different From Daily Medication

One of the most appealing features of gene therapy is the possibility of achieving lasting results without repeated treatments.

Traditional medicines generally work only as long as patients continue taking them. Genomic therapies operate differently because they act on genetic material itself. They may provide a healthy version of a gene, suppress a gene responsible for harmful effects, or modify a specific DNA sequence.

This makes it possible to develop treatments intended to work after a single dose. Such therapies are often called "one-and-done" treatments.

However, receiving a treatment only once does not necessarily mean its effects will last a lifetime.

Smith explains that many gene therapies use modified viruses to carry genetic instructions into cells. The immune system can recognize these delivery vehicles and develop a response against them. As a result, administering the same treatment again may be difficult or impossible, even if its benefits begin to fade.

Another important distinction concerns which cells are changed. Current gene therapies generally target somatic cells, which are the body's cells other than those involved in reproduction. Unlike germline editing, these treatments are not intended to create genetic changes that can be inherited by future generations.

Why Gene Editing Common Diseases Raises New Risks

For people living with rare, devastating genetic conditions, the benefits of gene therapy may clearly outweigh the potential dangers. Some patients have few effective treatment options, making even an experimental intervention worth considering.

The situation becomes considerably more complicated when the same technology is used against common diseases.

Conditions such as high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes already have established treatments. Many of these medications can be adjusted as a patient's condition changes or discontinued if troublesome side effects develop.

A permanent genetic intervention may not offer that flexibility.

Murthy also points to a major concern involving the number of people who might eventually receive these treatments. A serious side effect that occurs only rarely could still harm a substantial number of patients if a therapy is administered to millions.

For that reason, treatments intended for widespread use must meet especially demanding safety standards.

Five Questions Scientists Say Must Be Answered

To help determine when genomic therapy is appropriate, Smith and Murthy propose evaluating five essential factors:

The final question may be especially challenging.

Clinical trials typically involve relatively small groups of patients who are monitored for limited periods. Although these studies can identify many important safety concerns, they may miss extremely rare complications or problems that take years to develop.

Some adverse effects might only become apparent after a treatment has reached a much larger population.

The Problem of Tracking Risks That Could Emerge Years Later

Smith argues that long-term monitoring cannot be treated as an afterthought. It needs to be an essential part of how gene therapies are introduced into medical practice.

Patient registries, which collect information about people receiving particular treatments, have already shown how valuable extended follow-up can be.

However, therapies that could eventually reach millions of patients will require monitoring systems capable of operating on a much larger scale.

These systems must be independent and standardized so researchers can consistently evaluate whether treatments remain effective and whether unexpected health problems appear over time.

Without reliable long-term data, doctors may struggle to determine the full consequences of genetic interventions that cannot easily be reversed.

Could Some Genetic Changes Be Too Risky to Make Permanent?

Another concern is whether certain diseases or biological processes are suitable for permanent treatment at all.

Murthy emphasizes that developing the ability to alter a genetic target does not automatically make doing so the best medical decision.

Some conditions require careful adjustments to medication doses over time. In other cases, the difference between an effective treatment and a harmful one can be extremely small. Changing a biological process too much or too little could create serious complications.

Conventional medications offer an important advantage in these situations because doctors can modify or stop treatment as needed.

Permanent gene therapies generally lack that option.

Scientists may eventually overcome this limitation by developing genetic treatments with built-in biological "off-switches" or other methods for reversing their effects.

Until those approaches have been shown to work reliably, the ability to undo or adjust a treatment remains an important safety advantage of traditional medicine.

The Million-Dollar Challenge Facing Gene Therapy

Safety is not the only barrier to bringing gene editing into mainstream healthcare. Cost could also determine whether these treatments become widely available.

Some existing gene therapies have list prices above $1 million for a single patient, and several cost substantially more.

Such prices may be considered justifiable for certain rare, life-threatening conditions, particularly when treatment options are extremely limited.

But applying similar pricing to diseases affecting millions of people would place enormous financial pressure on healthcare systems.

Smith and Murthy argue that affordability and access must therefore be part of the discussion from the beginning.

Even a highly effective gene therapy could create new healthcare inequalities if only a small percentage of patients could obtain it. Researchers and policymakers must consider not just whether these treatments work, but also whether they can be delivered without making existing disparities worse.

Could One Gene-Editing Treatment Prevent Heart Disease for Decades?

Despite these challenges, the possibility of using gene editing to prevent common diseases is becoming increasingly realistic.

Researchers are already conducting early studies to investigate whether a single genetic treatment can produce long-lasting reductions in LDL, commonly known as "bad," cholesterol.

LDL cholesterol contributes to the buildup of fatty deposits inside arteries, which can increase the risk of heart attacks and other cardiovascular problems. Lowering LDL over extended periods is an important strategy for reducing cardiovascular risk.

If gene editing can safely produce sustained reductions, it could eventually offer a new approach to protecting cardiovascular health without requiring patients to take medication indefinitely.

However, promising early results will not be enough to justify widespread use.

Before these therapies become routine options for common conditions, researchers will need convincing evidence that their benefits last, their risks remain acceptably low over many years, and their costs are manageable. Reliable safeguards will also be essential.

For Smith and Murthy, the objective is not to hold back genetic medicine. It is to make sure that a technology with the potential to transform healthcare is introduced carefully and responsibly.

As gene therapy moves beyond rare disorders toward conditions affecting millions of people, the central challenge will be ensuring that the promise of lasting protection does not come at the expense of long-term patient safety.

#825. Stacy Keach, Mike Hammer and Blue Bloods Star, Dead at 85

Mike Hammer's Stacy Keach died at age 85 after a battle with a serious heart condition, his wife Malgosia Tomassi shared on Nov. 10.

The Mike Hammer alum died after a "long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure" at his family home in Magdalenka, Poland, his wife Malgosia Tomassi confirmed. He was 85.

"Stacy peacefully departed this world," she wrote in a Nov. 10 statement obtained by People. "He fought for so long, with extraordinary courage, determination and strength. He was a true warrior, facing his illness with the same remarkable spirit and resilience that defined his life."

Tomassi—with whom Keach shared son Shannon and daughter Karolina—reflected on her husband's golden life and his most award-winning roles: dad and husband of 40 years.

"Stacy was not only a legendary actor, admired and loved by audiences the world over, but also my beloved husband, my companion and the heart of our family," she continued. "His passing leaves an immeasurable emptiness in our lives. But his extraordinary spirit, his unforgettable voice and the love he gave so generously will remain with us forever."

Keach, born in 1941 to Mary Caine and theater director and actor Stacy Keach Sr., simply followed in his parents' acting footsteps.

"It started with my family really," he recalled on the Let's Dive In podcast in October 2020. "My dad, God love him, was an actor. My mom studied acting even though she never went into it professionally. I grew up in a theatrical family."

But that's not to say Caine and Keach Sr. were too keen on their son catching the acting bug.

"My parents did not want me to become an actor," he admitted. "Having been in the business, they thought it was an insecure profession. It's fraught with heartache."

Nevertheless, though they hoped Keach would pursue law or medicine, he knew he was meant to be on the stage and in front of a camera. So, after acting in school plays at age 12, he began his professional acting career at age 20 with roles on the stage at the 1962 Oregon Shakespeare Festival in The Comedy of Errors, Henry IV Part 2 and Coriolanus.

Appearing in several Broadway, Off-Broadway and local shows, he earned a Best Actor Tony nomination and Drama Desk Award for 1970's Indian. Keach—often lauded for his roles in William Shakespeare plays, including Hamlet and Macbeth—was also inducted into the Theater Hall of Fame in 2015.

While he continued in theater until 2018's Pamplona, he also earned several television roles, beginning with 1964's Channing before stepping into film with the 1967 TV movie The Winter's Tale. His first main character role came in 1997 as private investigator Mike Hammer in the titular series. He also appeared as a recurring character on Blue Bloods as Archbishop Kevin Kearns from 2016 to 2024.

Keach proved he was a jack of all trades, making his silver screen debut in 1968's The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter as Jake Blount. He even narrated The Duellists, Ridley Scott's directorial debut, in 1977. He would go on to star in other projects like Fat City, Up in Smoke and American History X. His final role was in 2025's Jay Kelly as the father of George Clooney's titular character.

Looking back at his career, the actor opted to focus on the positives, rather than any potential missed opportunities.

"I try not to dwell on mistakes and wallow in regret," he reflected in his 2013 memoir All in All: An Actor's Life On and Off the Stage. "If a script interests me, or a character intrigues me, or the cast features someone I've always wanted to work with, or the location is somewhere exotic, then sign me up."

"Starlog" was one of the greatest sci-fi and fantasy magazines ever, and after a 17-year absence, it's being resurrected.

The legendary sci-fi mag went dark back in 2009 as part of the wave of popular publications folding due to years of declining readership and subscriptions. But as of Nov. 13, this geek favorite periodical returns as an annual print edition, and it's available for pre-order now.

It’s another indication of digital fatigue in the world, and fans of a certain age will recall the pleasure of poring over each colorful issue packed with in-depth interviews, behind-the-scenes photos, TV guides, classic movie retrospectives, book reviews, con news, and VFX features.

"Starlog" launched in 1976, in the pre-"Star Wars" days, under the leadership of editor-in-chief Kerry O’Quinn. It first arrived with artist Jack Thurston's beautiful painted "Star Trek" cover, featuring William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk and Leonard Nimoy’s Spock, set against the U.S.S. Enterprise near a shimmering black hole.

The magazine continued to inform the science fiction community about upcoming sci-fi TV shows and blockbuster Hollywood films for over three decades; I fondly recall reading each informative and entertaining monthly issue cover-to-cover.

Just in time to honor its 50th anniversary this year, "Starlog" blasts back into the sci-fi universe with Issue #375 showcasing cover artwork created by Armenian artist Gabriel Yeganyan. Its geek culture legacy, covering iconic franchises like "Star Wars," "Star Trek," and "Alien," will now live on thanks to Fangoria Holdings and io9 co-founder Annalee Newitz, editor-in-chief.

"During its original 33-year run, 'Starlog' documented science fiction as it evolved across film, television, books, technology, and culture," said 'Fangoria's Tara Ansley.

"Fifty years after the magazine first launched, the line between science fiction and the real world has become increasingly difficult to separate. That makes this an especially interesting time to bring 'Starlog' back. Technology may change, but the most compelling questions have always been about people: how we live, what we create, and what kind of future we want to build."

"Starlog" reloads for its first annual edition after a long hiatus on Nov. 13. You can pre-order the first issue (Issue 375 in continuity) on the Starlog website.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

#823. Shirt pull on Isak should have been penalty - panel

Alexander Isak (centre) has scored seven goals in nine Premier League games for Liverpool this season

Liverpool should have been awarded a penalty against Arsenal after Alexander Isak was pulled back by Jurrien Timber, the Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel has ruled.

Isak just failed to get his head on the end of a cross by Bradley Barcola in the 21st minute of the game at Anfield on 1 November.

Referee Andy Madley did not award a penalty and it was checked and cleared by video assistant referee (VAR) Stuart Attwell, but replays showed Timber grabbed Isak's shirt.

The KMI Panel voted 4:1 that the penalty should have been awarded on the field, with a 3:2 vote that the VAR should have intervened and sent the referee to the pitchside monitor.

Arsenal led 1-0 at the time through Kai Havertz, which proved to be the only goal of the game.

Two panellists highlighted the "subjectivity in assessing impact" as a reason not to intervene, but the majority view was that it was a "clear and obvious error" by the VAR.

The KMI Panel unanimously voted that Timber's challenge did not warrant a red card for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity.

Isak stayed on his feet during the incident.

After the match, Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola told BBC Match of the Day: "There is a clear grab of the shirt.

"Alex was just in front of him. He was going to head in front of the goal, but couldn't because he grabbed the shirt.

"If he goes to the floor, they call the penalty, 100%. It should be like this, but it is what it is.

"Next time, the managers should tell Alex to go to the floor, otherwise they won't call it.

"The answer is you have to dive. If you don't dive they won't call it."

The KMI Panel ruled that there was a second VAR error on 31 October.

It said Ipswich should have been awarded a penalty against Hull City when Nobel Mendy held back Dara O'Shea at a corner.

Referee Peter Bankes did not spot the offence and VAR Neil Davies took no action.

The game was 0-0 at the time. Ipswich took the lead shortly afterwards and it finished 2-2.

#822. The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but new research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.

In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.

"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," said senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD."

How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear

To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.

The researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.

At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.

"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," said Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.

Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger

Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an important evolutionary purpose.

The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.

Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.

"The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters."

The ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.

A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD

The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.

For someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.

The researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.

"Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," said Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'."

Because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.

The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.

The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

#821. Even giant anteaters in remote Brazil have microplastics in their blood

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gemma Conroy is a freelance journalist in Mexico City and editor of Nature Briefing: Careers.

Giant anteaters traipsing across Brazil's pristine wetlands and savannas have ingested traces of plastic pollutants. Credit: Sylvain Cordier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty

Some of Brazil’s wildlife have traces of plastic circulating in their blood — even if they live far from land used by humans, according to an analysis published on 11 November in Nature1.

Researchers measured the concentration of microplastics in the blood of 47 animals: 26 lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) and 21 giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla). The scientists found that, on average, the creatures carry similar levels of plastic to many humans — roughly 74 particles per millilitre of blood. The animals that lived closest to human infrastructure and waste-management facilities had the highest levels of microplastics in their blood.

But even those living more than 100 kilometres from a waste sites and 65 kilometres from human infrastructure showed traces of the pollutants. This indicates that plastics can reach wildlife living far from where the pollution originates, says study co-author Marcia de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz, a conservation scientist at the University of British Columbia, Okanagan in Kelowna, Canada.

The findings are an important step to better understand how the particles impact wildlife, says Sofia Ya-Hsuan Liou, a geochemist at the National Taiwan University in Taipei.

Microplastics are tiny particles (smaller than five millimetres) with many different chemical compositions. They can travel through the environment in rainwater, rivers and the atmosphere. Although several studies have measured microplastics in wildlife, few have explored how the surrounding environment influences what animals ingest, says study co-author Michael Noonan, a quantitative ecologist at the University of British Columbia Okanagan.

To find out, Noonan, Ferraz and their colleagues collected and analysed blood samples from animals living across the Amazon rainforest, the Cerrado savanna and the huge and pristine Pantanal wetland between February 2021 and November 2022. The researchers also used GPS data to track the animals’ movements and their exposure to human footprint.

#820. Turkey-based Bates replaces Binks in Scotland squad

David Bates could add to his four Scotland caps

Centre-back David Bates could win his first cap in seven years after being added to the Scotland squad for the matches against North Macedonia and Switzerland.

Bates, playing with Amedspor in Turkey, won the last of his four Scotland caps in 2019 and replaces fellow defender Luis Binks, who has withdrawn.

As well as spells in his homeland, 30-year-old Bates has club experience in Belgium, England and Germany, with most appearances coming at Mechelen.

He has started all 11 matches this season as Amedspor sit third in the Turkish Super Lig.

All of Bates' Scotland outings came under Alex McLeish while playing for Hamburg in the 2018-19 campaign.

Luke Graham, Jack Hendry and Ryan Porteous are the other central defenders in Sebastien Pocognoli's squad, though left-back Kieran Tierney can also operate in the head coach's preferred back three.

Brondby's Binks won his first three caps during Scotland's opening four Nations League fixtures, in which they picked up four points.

North Macedonia, who travel to Hampden on Friday, have no points in the section, with Slovenia three points better off than Scotland and Monday's hosts Switzerland on maximum points.

"Our tiny ground station shouted at an ESA spacecraft, and was heard."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A satellite went knee-deep in the dead, after a voice command from the ground activated the Doom video game in space.

Playing a first-person shooter from 1993 was obviously not in the design plan for the PRETTY cubesat, which is run by a consortium including the European Space Agency (ESA). But the pioneering voice command opens up new worlds for satellite work, the team says.

"Someone in distress at sea or in a remote area could transmit 'mayday' or "help" on a radio," stated Estonia's Tanagra Space, which supplied the software for the feat. The hope is one day, a satellite could use transcription and AI to alert rescue services for assisting folks in remote zones.

The call to play Doom, thankfully, had no other urgency than curiosity — and teamwork, fueled by pizza. OPS-SAT Space Lab managed the experiment on behalf of ESA. Radio amateurs then made six unsuccessful attempts during passes over Poland and Norway, between April and July. The seventh finally reached success under the Oslo Group of the Norwegian Radio Relay League.

"We are radio amateurs, with the emphasis on amateurs. Satellite work was not something our club did, and we had no budget for it," representative Eskil Hadland, call sign LB6AJ, said in the Tangara statement. "So we borrowed a line wrongly credited to Pippi Longstocking: 'I have never tried that before, so I should definitely be able to do that.'"

The Norwegians spent 59 days and about 7200 NOK or $775 (pizza included) to reach PRETTY, helping make changes to the satellite software to pick up a voice. For example, a raw recording of an attempt on July 3, retransmitted to Earth, showed the spoken words to space were unrecognizable. Further work revealed the satellite's receiver channel was too wide to pick up the voice signal, leading to a fix to narrow the channel.

The historic voice command on July 27— in part, "PRETTY play Doom Doom Doom"— came from a rooftop in Oslo, and was spoken at night by Jon Bergli Heier (LB9BJ). PRETTY picked up the transmission, transcribed the command using on-board voice recognition, and then — just like a typical evening gamer—opened up Doom for a play session.

This was no multiplayer gaming situation, but the satellite did create a report of its demon-slaying skills — and its ability to interpret the command. For example, PRETTY generated a "postcard" including a frame of the gameplay, a transcription, and signal diagnostics. The satellite also transmitted its recording of Hadland's command.

As anybody who uses voice-recognition software knows, there are challenges in transcriptions: nobody speaks in exactly the same way, and aspects such as accent or background noise can lead to misinterpretations. The satellite also had to contend with Doppler shift, and with an antenna not designed to relay voices to space.

But the transmission clearly worked, powered by open-source tools including GNU Radio (which handled the signal processing) and Sherpa-ONNX (speech recognition).

The hope is that future spacecraft could one day adapt this approach to radio frequencies for other ideas outside of spoken words. For example, perhaps deep-space radio signals could be detected via satellite, with an AI on board sending the most relevant data to operators after analyzing the work.

For now, however, the Norwegian radio operators are basking in the success: "Our tiny ground station shouted at an ESA spacecraft, and was heard," Hadland said.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#818. How Lauren Sánchez Bezos Handles Criticism Amid Life With Jeff Bezos

Lauren Sánchez Bezos revealed how she handles negative comments surrounding her marriage to Jeff Bezos as well as her appearance: “I’m human. I get my feelings hurt just like anyone else.”

Lauren Sánchez Bezos is focusing on the big picture.

The former Good Day L.A. anchor—who tied the knot with husband Jeff Bezos in 2025—revealed her secret to blocking out the haters, especially when it comes to criticism of her marriage and lifestyle.

“I’m human. I get my feelings hurt just like anyone else,” Lauren admitted during a Nov. 10 appearance on CBS Mornings. “But I think in this world there’s so much noise and you can’t let it get into your heart and you have to focus on the things that are really important.”

And for the 56-year-old, the issue on her mind is childhood education.

“One right now is focusing on kids with a learning difference,” she explained. “It really is important. And parents should know this that you can get your kids tested. So, if you’re in a public school and you think your kid is struggling, you just have to write a letter to your teacher and to the principal and they have to test your kid.”

She emphasized. “I stay focused on that.”

The mission is a personal one for Lauren, who’s used her experience with dyslexia as the foundation for a series of children’s books starring Flynn the Fly.

In fact, Lauren—mom to son Nikko, 25, with ex Tony Gonzalez as well as kids Evan, 20, and Ella, 18, with ex-husband Patrick Whitesell—just released her third book titled The Fly Who Flew to the North Pole.

“Flynn the fly is back—and this time, Christmas is on the line,” a synopsis for the book reads. “When her best friend Rio, a reindeer, gets chosen for Santa’s navigator training, it’s the moment he’s been dreaming of his whole life.”

“But Rio is worried: The numbers and directions keep jumbling on the page. Nothing stays still. And the test is tomorrow,” the description added. “Flynn knows that feeling. So she does what best friends do—help!”

Lauren released the first book in her The Fly Who Flew series in 2024. At the time, the philanthropist admitted she wasn’t buzzing over the idea of having her work up for public scrutiny.

"Having the spotlight on me is a little nerve-wracking," she told People that year. "I'd rather be on the other end. I'm very curious and I love asking questions. People are like, 'We haven't heard you talk in public much, and I'm like—but I was talking for 15 years on television!"

But she credited her learning difference with helping her develop tough skin.

"I think dyslexia has given me resilience," she said. "When you have dyslexia, you're so used to failing at things and it can be extremely humiliating. Especially as a young kid. But once you get through that, nothing can stop you."

"People want to put you in a box," Lauren continued. "But we don't thrive in boxes. Life is about trying new things."

Black tie preferred at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party in March 2023.

They made a night of it in New York at the ICCF U.S. Congressional International Conservation Leadership Awards Dinner on Oct. 24, 2023.

Lauren wore a "shattered glass" gown by Oscar de la Renta to the 2024 Met Gala, the couple's first time attending fashion's premiere event together.

Lauren's fall 2024 photo dump featured this sweet gem.

Jeff paid tribute to Lauren on her 55th birthday Dec. 19, 2024, with a photo celebrating the release of The Fly Who Flew to Space—which rocketed right onto the New York Times Best Seller List.

"What an incredible year — you set your mind to writing a children’s book and now you’re a NYT best selling author," he wrote on Instagram. "I have a feeling your next trip around the sun will be just as amazing. Happy birthday, baby!"

The power couple were among the VIPs who secured a prime viewing position to watch President Donald Trump be sworn in for a second time on Jan. 20, 2025.

Following the 97th Academy Awards on March 2, 2025, Jeff and Lauren stepped out for the annual Vanity Fair Oscars Party, where she wore a bridal-inspired Oscar de la Renta gown.

As Lauren set off on the all-female Blue Origin space flight alongside Gayle King, Katy Perry, former NASA rocket scientist Aisha Bowe, activist Amanda Nguyen and producer Kerianne Flynn, Jeff—who founded the space tech company in 2000—was right there to escort his fiancée aboard the rocket.

“I’m so excited for you, I don’t wanna get off,” he said before the takeoff on April 14, 2025. “I wanna go with you.”

#817. Dead stars could break one of physics' most famous limits

Some of the universe's dead stars may be capable of growing far more massive than a famous limit in physics was thought to allow. New computer simulations suggest that powerful magnetic fields hidden inside these stellar remnants could help them withstand crushing gravity and reach extraordinary masses.

The discovery challenges a long-standing understanding of white dwarfs, the dense cores left behind when certain stars exhaust their nuclear fuel and shed their outer layers. Although these stellar remnants are roughly the size of Earth, they can contain as much mass as the Sun or even more.

For white dwarfs without strong magnetic fields or rapid rotation, physicists have long recognized an upper mass boundary of approximately 1.4 times the Sun's mass. Known as the Chandrasekhar limit, this threshold plays an important role in understanding how some stars end their lives in spectacular explosions.

When a white dwarf made primarily of carbon and oxygen approaches this limit, the increasing pressure and density inside its core can ignite carbon, potentially setting off a powerful thermonuclear explosion known as a Type Ia supernova.

Scientists Discover How Magnetic Fields Could Break a Famous Cosmic Limit

New simulations by researchers from the Department of Physics at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and their collaborators suggest that the traditional mass limit may not apply to white dwarfs with sufficiently strong internal magnetic fields.

In one simulation, a magnetized white dwarf reached approximately 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, substantially exceeding the conventional limit of 1.4 solar masses.

"The idea started in 2011, when a summer student came to me and I gave him a problem quite casually: to check whether the Chandrasekhar limit can be violated by a magnetic field," explains Banibrata Mukhopadhyay, Professor at the Department of Physics and corresponding author of the study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The possibility of white dwarfs exceeding the Chandrasekhar limit is not entirely new. Theoretical physicists have explored these unusual objects, sometimes called "super-Chandrasekhar" white dwarfs, for decades.

Astronomers have also observed Type Ia supernovae that shine much more brightly than expected. These exceptionally luminous explosions have raised the possibility that some white dwarfs may reach masses as high as 2.8 times that of the Sun before exploding.

However, demonstrating that such massive white dwarfs could theoretically exist is only part of the challenge. Scientists also need to explain how an ordinary star could naturally develop into one.

Following a Star's Evolution From Birth to Death

"The important question was not simply whether a super-Chandrasekhar white dwarf is possible, but whether a star can actually evolve into one," says Zenia Zuraiq, first author of the study and PhD student at the Department of Physics. "Our simulations allowed us to follow that evolutionary pathway from the main-sequence star to the white dwarf, and show that under certain conditions, such a pathway is possible."

To investigate this process, the researchers modified a stellar evolution computer program called STARS, originally developed at the University of Cambridge.

The team expanded the software to account for magnetic fields and the cooling of white dwarfs. These additions allowed them to simulate how magnetized stars change over time, beginning with the main-sequence stage, when stars generate energy by fusing hydrogen into helium.

The simulations then followed the stars through their later evolutionary stages and into their final state as white dwarfs. Afterward, the researchers modeled a binary star system in which a white dwarf gradually pulls matter from a neighboring companion star.

This process, known as accretion, allows the white dwarf to gain mass over time. The researchers wanted to determine whether its growing magnetic field could change how much additional material it could support.

A Hidden Magnetic Force Helps Dead Stars Resist Gravity

The simulations revealed a surprising effect. Even a magnetic field that starts out relatively weak can become increasingly influential as a white dwarf accumulates matter.

As material builds up, the star becomes denser and contracts under its own gravity. This compression strengthens its internal magnetic field, which in turn provides additional pressure that helps counteract gravity.

The stronger magnetic support allows the white dwarf to hold more mass than would otherwise be possible. It also changes the familiar relationship between a white dwarf's mass and its size, potentially creating different maximum mass limit(s) depending on how magnetic fields behave inside the star.

One simulation illustrates just how dramatic the difference could be.

The researchers modeled a carbon-oxygen white dwarf with an initial mass of 1.02 times that of the Sun. It had formed from a main-sequence star that originally contained eight solar masses.

In the simulation, the white dwarf gradually accumulated material from its companion at a rate of 10⁻⁹ solar masses per year, equivalent to one billionth of the Sun's mass annually.

When magnetic effects were included, the white dwarf could reach approximately 2.4 solar masses. Without those effects, an otherwise comparable model reached the conventional limit of roughly 1.4 solar masses.

The results suggest that magnetic fields could fundamentally alter how massive a white dwarf can become.

The same mechanism may also help explain another astronomical puzzle. Some well-studied white dwarfs have unexpectedly large radii for their relatively low masses. Magnetic pressure could provide a possible explanation for why these stars appear larger than conventional models predict.

Could the Discovery Change How We Measure the Universe?

The implications could extend well beyond the evolution of dying stars.

Type Ia supernovae are among astronomy's most important tools for measuring distances across the cosmos. Because their peak brightness can be standardized, astronomers use them as cosmic reference points, often called standardizable candles.

By comparing how bright these explosions actually are with how bright they appear from Earth, researchers can estimate their distances. Such measurements have helped scientists investigate the universe's size, history, and ongoing expansion.

The Chandrasekhar limit has traditionally provided an important part of the physical framework for understanding these explosions. If white dwarfs reach similar masses before exploding, their energy output and brightness can be expected to follow broadly predictable patterns.

However, the new findings suggest that some exploding white dwarfs could have substantially different masses and internal magnetic fields.

Those differences could influence the properties and luminosity of the resulting supernovae, potentially helping explain why certain Type Ia explosions are unusually bright.

Understanding how magnetic fields affect these stellar explosions could therefore help astronomers refine their interpretations of supernova brightness and improve their understanding of cosmic expansion.

Although the findings come from computer simulations rather than direct observations of white dwarfs growing to these extreme masses, they offer a possible evolutionary pathway for stars that exceed the traditional Chandrasekhar limit.

The research suggests that one of astronomy's most famous mass limits may have important exceptions, with powerful magnetic fields allowing some dead stars to become far heavier than previously expected.

#816. Does Pickford finally face serious competition for his England place?

England head coach Thomas Tuchel used long-time first choice Jordan Pickford (left) and James Trafford (right) during the previous international break

When England head coach Thomas Tuchel decided to pick Leeds United goalkeeper James Trafford to face World Cup holders Spain at Wembley in the last international break, it sparked the first stirrings about preparations for life without long-time first choice Jordan Pickford.

Tuchel made it clear Pickford was still England's number one pick, but the simple fact he decided to alternate keepers - playing Trafford in the 3-2 loss to Spain then victory against Czech Republic, before Everton's 32-year-old returned for the Wembley win against the Czechs and the 7-0 rout in Croatia - created intrigue and debate.

England meet Croatia at Wembley on Thursday before facing the biggest test of their Uefa Nations League campaign when they play Spain in Madrid on Sunday.

Tuchel maintains strong faith in Pickford, an outstanding performer for England, but Trafford has at least had the chance to stake his claim.

Tuchel has suggested he may use a rotation system for the pair once more in the upcoming internationals, which will only increase scrutiny on England's goalkeeping position.

Pickford's record is outstanding since he made his debut in a 0-0 draw against Germany at Wembley in 2017.

In his time as first choice, England have once more emerged as major players on global stage, reaching the World Cup semi-finals in 2018 and 2026, as well as successive Euros finals at the delayed 2020 tournament and Euro 2024.

Measured by Opta stats, Pickford has made only two errors leading to goals in 93 appearances, with 46 clean sheets and a 74% save ratio.

Trafford's international career is in its infancy and, while former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson says Pickford remains Tuchel's undisputed first choice, he believes the head coach's recent strategy is a sensible one.

Robinson told BBC Sport: "It obviously remains to be seen what Thomas Tuchel does in these two England games, but I could see exactly what he was doing by giving James Trafford game time in the last round of matches.

"We are so guilty as a nation of taking one goalkeeper to a tournament who has 70, 80, 90 caps, then the two of three below him could have less than double figures combined."

Robinson's point is proved by the statistic that 80 of Pickford's appearances have been competitive games, with 33 at major tournaments, made up of 19 at the World Cup and 14 at European Championships.

"Competitive and tournament caps give you the type of experience you can't get as a number two or three keeper," said Robinson.

"James Trafford is only 24 and has four caps - two of them competitive - so you can see exactly what Tuchel is doing, looking ahead to a situation where England's recognised number one is not available to him, or there is a drop off in form.

"We saw the last selections and all thought Jordan Pickford's place is under threat and James Trafford is going to be the next number one. I don't think Thomas Tuchel saw it as starkly or simply as that.

"It's a conversation that will definitely take place down the road, but not now. Jordan is England's first choice, in my opinion, rightfully so given his consistency and performances over such a long period.

"This is a debate and conversation for the future definitely because Father Time catches up with everyone eventually and the manager needs to have a contingency plan, but Jordan Pickford very much remains number one and Thomas Tuchel has said as much.

"I don't think Jordan Pickford is under threat for his jersey on a permanent basis any time soon, irrespective of the next selection, but what Tuchel is doing reinforces the impression that he has to be at the top of his game and maintain high standards, which he certainly has been doing when I've watched him this season.

"The biggest compliment I can pay Jordan Pickford is that when you have got that England goalkeeper's shirt, everybody thinks somebody else should be doing it. I know that from personal experience.

"You're there to be shot at, but there has been no noise around Jordan Pickford for a very long time now.

"It has worked both ways for Jordan, James and Thomas Tuchel, and worked very well. Jordan knows he can't rest on his laurels and he will just play regardless. He has to be playing well.

"Is James Trafford challenging Jordan Pickford right now? Yes he is - if Jordan Pickford isn't playing very well and Jordan Pickford is making errors.

"None of the above are true right now because he's playing well for Everton and has done nothing wrong for England."

Robinson also drew on club form to support Pickford's case. Since the start of the 2024-25 season, only Arsenal's title-winning keeper David Raya has more clean sheets in the league than Pickford at Everton.

Raya has 39 clean sheets in that time, while Pickford has 27, with Robinson saying: "That's a superb record and all logic tells you Pickford will have to work a lot harder for his clean sheets than David Raya."

Trafford staked his claim in those Nations League games against Spain and the Czech Republic, putting him at the forefront of Tuchel's thoughts as the main understudy to Pickford.

Crystal Palace's Dean Henderson is now back in contention after injury and hoping to add to his six caps, although he has not been included in Tuchel's latest squad.

Trafford moved to Leeds United from Manchester City in the summer in a British record deal for a goalkeeper that could be worth up to Â£45m.

It came after a Â£23m move to City from Burnley the previous summer, when his hopes of becoming Pep Guardiola's first choice were unexpectedly ended by the decision to sign Gianluigi Donnarumma from Paris St-Germain.

Robinson said: "James Trafford needed that move to Leeds United and Leeds United needed a keeper of his level. This is a match made in heaven.

"And don't forget, in a Premier League career with Burnley, Manchester City and Leeds United, Trafford has only played 42 Premier League games â just a little more than a full season â and one Champions League game. He needs this experience.

"He's got a huge amount of potential, with his quality, all-round goalkeeping and mental approach. He has the potential be England's future number one, which Tuchel clearly sees him to be.

"He has the mentality to reach the very top, which is very difficult because not all goalkeepers have that. It's a tough place to be, a very lonely place to be, but he has the ability to cope with that situation.

"I was at Bournemouth when he made an error in the Leeds United defeat there, but, knowing the type of character he, is it won't faze him. It won't bother him. Because of his personality and his character traits, he has got the ability to go right to the top.

"You'd think Dean Henderson will be back in the squad in due course once he has played more games.

"Jason Steele is in there again, but he's a mentor figure behind the scenes, not someone who will ever start or threaten the established goalkeepers.

"If you rewind back 18 or 24 months, you had Nick Pope, Sam Johnstone, James Trafford, Dean Henderson, Aaron Ramsdale and Jordan Pickford - a real plethora of England goalkeepers.

"Now Nick Pope is not playing at Newcastle United, Sam Johnstone's not in the equation and Aaron Ramsdale is nowhere near."

Ramsdale's decline has been dramatic after leaving Arsenal for Southampton in August 2024, with a loan spell at Newcastle United proving to be unsuccessful. He has effectively been fourth choice at Saints this season, failing to make matchday squads.

Robinson said: "I find Aaron Ramsdale's situation very sad because I believe he's a goalkeeper able to play at the top level.

"He should be in this conversation because he's a goalkeeper I really like, but he's been very unfortunate with selection of clubs and the way their season have gone. I still think there is time for him to come back into the reckoning.

"For now, though, if there is a conversation to be had about England's goalkeepers, then Jordan Pickford and James Trafford is that conversation, with Jordan still very much the number one right now as far as I'm concerned."

#815. Antonio Sabáto Jr., Virginia Madsen’s Son Arrested After Fatal Crash

Antonio Sabáto Jr. and Virginia Madsen’s son Jack Sabáto was arrested in Anchorage, Alaska after a pedestrian was struck by a vehicle in the early hours of Nov. 9.

Antonio Sabáto Jr. and Virgina Madsen’s son is facing legal trouble.

The son of the former couple, Jack Sabáto, was arrested in Anchorage, Alaska Nov. 9 in relation to a hit-and-run incident that killed 42-year-old pedestrian Carl Simmonds earlier that same morning, local authorities confirmed in a press release.

Sabáto, 32, was arrested on charges of leaving the scene of an accident without assisting the injured and leaving the scene of an accident resulting in injury or death. He was taken into custody at the Anchorage Correctional Complex, E! News confirmed.

Authorities opened the investigation into Simmonds’ death around 5:48 a.m. local time in Anchorage, after patrol officers and medics responded to reports of an unresponsive male at the intersection of Airport Heights drive and Debarr road in Anchorage. The preliminary investigation indicated that the adult male pedestrian had been struck by a vehicle which fled the scene.

Police report documents obtained by KTUU indicate that officers located a vehicle—a white Chevrolet Tahoe—involved in the crash that was registered to Sabáto’s home address. On the afternoon of Nov. 9, police found the vehicle parked at Sabáto’s place of work and saw that it had “fresh damage to the right front corner that was consistent with a pedestrian strike.”

Later in the afternoon, around 2:45 local time, Sabáto called authorities himself to say he believed he had hit an animal with his car and wanted to speak with officers. Sabáto alleged that he had been “doing late night DoorDashing” when “something suddenly appeared in the road.”

In the documents, Sabáto noted that he knew he hit “something” while driving but didn’t want to check because he does not have car insurance. He also told authorities that he called in the report because he “knew the worst.”

Sabáto was arraigned on Nov. 10 and his bail was set at $5,000, plus a no-driving order and an additional $5,000 penalty if he fails to appear at future court dates. He remained in custody as of the morning of Nov. 11, police confirmed to E! News.

Following his son's arrest, The Big Hit alum said his family was "navigating an estremely sensitive and deeply personal matter" in a statement on his social media Nov. 11.

Regarding the death of Simmonds, Sabáto Jr. added, "I also wish to extend my heartfelt condolences to the family and loved ones of the gentleman who tragically lost his life."

E! News has reached out to representatives for Sabáto and his mother Madsen.

This post was updated to include the statement shared by Sabáto Jr., which was shared after publication.

#814. O'Shea proud of how team-mates handled Israel games

Dara O'Shea stepped in as Republic of Ireland captain for the last international window in place of the injured Nathan Collins

Republic of Ireland defender Dara O'Shea said he is "proud" of how he and his team-mates came through a trying October international window.

During a four-game Nations League schedule, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side lost away to Kosovo and drew at home to Austria - who they are preparing to face in return fixtures - but it was two games against Israel which tested their resolve.

O'Shea stepped in as captain in the absence of injured skipper Nathan Collins and the 27-year-old acknowledged it "was a tough situation to be in" as they faced Israel in two games on neutral territory.

The first of those resulted in a 3-0 victory for the Irish in Hungary, a game that looked in doubt the previous day when training was delayed as players took a vote on whether to play - amid protests over the Israel-Gaza war - with goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu making himself unavailable for selection.

The sides drew 1-1 in the second meeting in Serbia and, while the saga proved a challenge for all within the Republic of Ireland squad, O'Shea - who missed the second game for personal reasons - paid tribute to his team-mates for the support he received as stand-in skipper.

"I think I was quite lucky, I am really proud to be part of the group, with some great people in it," said the Ipswich Town captain.

"Even the players playing now as well, they are great leaders themselves. I never felt I was fully alone in having to do anything

"There were always people around me. I always keep level-headed, I don't get too high with the highs or too low with the lows."

He added: "Of course it was a difficult time, it was a time that I had to learn stuff about myself, how I was going to react to things. But I think as a group we did excellently.

"It was a tough situation to be in, but we overcame it as best we could. And I am really proud of the group and the staff."

Seamus Coleman has been without a club since leaving Everton at the end of last season

Collins is back to lead the team for Saturday's trip to face Austria in Linz and the final League B3 game at home to Kosovo on Tuesday (both 19:45 GMT).

Also part of the squad is Seamus Coleman, who has taken on a 'hybrid role' despite not being named in manager Hallgrimsson's official 24-man squad.

"It's great to have them [Collins and Coleman] back," O'Shea continued.

"It would have been great if they were there in the last camp as well, but we had some really good people in that last camp who were doing great things.

"Nathan's the captain, so it's always great to have him back in. Seamus' knowledge is so, so valuable to us. I think we are a stronger group when we have them two with us."

Coleman has been without a club since leaving Everton at the end of last season, following 17 years with the Toffees.

The 38-year-old defender recently said he is considering retirement but Republic of Ireland assistant coach John O'Shea is delighted to have the Donegal man around the squad.

"It's us helping Seamus and Seamus helping us," O'Shea said of Coleman's role on the training pitch.

"To see the impact he's having, the quality that remains in his ability and the driving and pushing he's doing for everyone in the group has been good to see. Not much has changed."

#813. 400,000-year-old teeth reveal a stunning twist in human evolution

For most of the 20th century, the model of human origins was a tree: with the trunk dividing into branches, and then twigs. Each species of human relative (hominin) was a neat, single branch.

As an undergraduate, I was taught that Homo sapiens was one of these branches that emerged in Africa, spread across the world, and displaced every archaic human it encountered.

Neanderthals, Homo erectus, and other ancient relatives were evolutionary dead ends – unfortunate cousins who left no descendants. In the 30 years since I left university, those early lessons are now radically revised.

That neat replacement story is now comprehensively wrong, largely thanks to studies like the one published in Nature by Qiaomei Fu from the Chinese Academy of Sciences and colleagues. The paper achieves something that would have seemed impossible a decade ago: it recovers meaningful biological information from H. erectus fossils far too old for DNA.

Instead of genetic sequences, the team extracted ancient proteins from the enamel of six teeth from three Chinese sites – Zhoukoudian (which, in the early 20th century, produced fossil remains known as “Peking Man”), Hexian and Sunjiadong – all dating to around 400,000 years ago.

Homo erectus is widely regarded as the first hominin to leave Africa; the evidence suggests this species had moved into Eurasia nearly two million years ago. It remains the most geographically widespread human ancestor that ever lived. The new study indicates that Homo erectus exchanged genes (probably through interbreeding) with Denisovans in East Asia roughly 400,000 years ago.

The study suggests that some of that genetic legacy, it now appears, was passed on to living people in the Philippines, Papua New Guinea, and across south-east Asia.

Tooth enamel is the hardest tissue in the body, and its proteins survive long after DNA has degraded beyond recovery. What the team found in those proteins is striking. All six specimens share a previously unknown amino acid variant – a tiny molecular signature, a single letter changed in the protein sequence, never seen in any other hominin alive or dead.

This variant clusters these east Asian H. erectus into a distinct group, confirming their identity and settling a long-running debate about whether the unusual Hexian fossils were H. erectus at all. A second variant they share, however, is not unique to H. erectus.

It also appears in Denisovans – a mysterious archaic (non-Homo sapiens) human group known mainly from a cave in Siberia. The corresponding genetic variant turns up in living people at frequencies of 21% in the Philippines and about 1% in India, distributed in a pattern that matches what we’d expect if it entered modern humans via Denisovan ancestry.

The most reasonable interpretation is that H. erectus populations in east Asia passed this variant to Denisovans through interbreeding, and Denisovans later passed it on to the ancestors of modern south-east Asians and Oceanians. This transfer of genetic material from one species to another is known as introgression.

The lineage we once thought was a dead end has, it turns out, left a small but detectable trace in living human genomes – a molecular thread connecting a Peking Man tooth to living people in Asia.

But the significance of today’s paper extends well beyond the specific variant or the specific populations involved. What it really shows is that interbreeding between archaic human lineages was not exceptional. It was routine.

Every major hominin lineage we have been able to examine genomically shows admixture. Modern humans outside Africa carry roughly 2% Neanderthal DNA. Papuans and Aboriginal Australians carry an additional 2–5% Denisovan ancestry.

West African populations carry genetic signatures from an unidentified archaic lineage. Even Denisovans themselves, as today’s study adds further weight to, received gene flow from something older and more diverged — likely H. erectus.

A 2019 review in the American Journal of Physical Anthropology documents at least three distinct introgression events from Denisovan-like populations into south-east Asian and Oceanic ancestors alone, some occurring as recently as 20,000 years ago. The picture is not one of clean lineages but of a tangled web of contact and exchange extending across millions of years.

The implications are far-reaching. Our genomes are not the product of a single unbroken lineage emerging from Africa. They are mosaics, assembled from contributions by multiple archaic groups, each adapted to its own regional environment.

Some of the Denisovan-derived variants in Papuan genomes, for instance, appear to influence immune function. The H. erectus-derived variant identified today has unknown functional consequences – that remains an open question – but the precedent from other gene variants that have introgressed (genes that have passed from one species into another) suggests that adaptation to new environments may have been part of the story.

Perhaps most intriguing is what the new paper implies about all the populations we cannot yet study. H. erectus survived in Indonesia until perhaps 100,000 years ago. Homo floresiensis, the diminutive “hobbit” species, was present on Flores when modern humans arrived. Another human lineage, Homo luzonensis, occupied the Philippines.

None of these populations have yielded DNA, and until today none had yielded any molecular data at all. Were they also absorbed, at least partially, into the human populations that replaced them? The genomic evidence from living people has not, so far, detected their signal clearly – but the tools available until recently were blunt instruments.

The proteomic approach demonstrated in today’s paper offers a way forward. If proteins can be recovered from H. erectus enamel at 400,000 years, the same approach applied to floresiensis or luzonensis material might finally reveal whether those lineages, too, contributed something to the humans who came after them.

The old metaphor of a tree – a single trunk branching into distinct species – has been quietly replaced in the scientific literature. It might be better to consider the process as a braided river, with many channels running partly together and partly apart, exchanging water continuously.

This new study is one more confirmation that when ancient human populations disappeared, they left traces of themselves behind.

#812. Trisha Paytas Reveals Jaw-Dropping YouTube Income She Made in a Week

Trisha Paytas, who first joined YouTube in 2007, revealed the six-figure amount she recently earned over seven days posting on the platform.

Trisha Paytas is just raking in the money off her kitchen floor.

After all, the Just Trish podcast host revealed the most money she’s earned from her YouTube channel in a single week.

"This week was a good week," Paytas said on the Nov. 10 episode of Watch What Happens Live with Andy Cohen alongside fellow guest Hailey Glassman. "Maybe $100K."

Since joining the platform in 2007, the 38-year-old—mom to kids Malibu, 4, Elvis, 2, and Aquaman, 15 months, with husband Moses Hacmon—admitted that her income has always fluctuated, especially after growing her family.

"It changes so much," she explained to Polyester Zine in 2023. "Before I was married, I'd wake up and I'd be filming five videos a day or something like that. Then when I got pregnant, I had a very easy schedule–I was just doing like ASMR, whatever felt good that day. But I really hustled right before I gave birth."

#811. NASA chief Jared Isaacman skydives into space agency's MAX POWER air show — 'Going into this job, I knew we had to do something like this.'

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman knows how to make an entrance. Under the bright afternoon sun on Saturday (Nov. 7), Isaacman plummeted through the air above 10,000 onlookers, skydiving into the agency's air show MAX POWER.

MAX POWER overtook NASA's Kennedy Space Center here over the weekend, combining aeronautics and aerospace in a massive public air show, the first of its kind for the space agency. A mix of astronauts, fighter jet displays and new technology on display, the spectacle is a lot space-ier than a traditional air show, and Isaacman made sure to really showcase this merging of worlds. A pilot and private astronaut, Jared Isaacman is no stranger to the skies, and immediately after landing back on solid ground he jumped right back up and took to the event's main stage to greet an excited crowd.

"Going into this job, I I knew we had to do something like this," Isaacman said after landing and taking the stage. "We knew on our nation's 250th birthday, we had to open up [the] Kennedy Space Center the year that we returned our astronauts to the lunar environment and put on a little bit of a show."

This mirrorless Canon has specs that make it one of the best cameras available right now, with impressive features and functionality, including a 45MP sensor and excellent high-ISO handling.

Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review.

From thousands of feet above a crowd holding their breath, Isaacman jumped out of a plane alongside members of Skydive Chicago and other notable individuals, including Montana senator Tim Sheehy (R-Montana) and former U.S. Air Force Thunderbird pilot Shawn Gustoson.

One by one, tiny white parachutes popped up in the sky above, which continued to grow in size as the skydivers neared the ground. And before we knew it, Isaacman was gracefully touching down just behind the air show's main stage, landing to the sound of cheers from the eager audience.

In addition to serving in his role as NASA Administrator, Isaacman is an entrepreneur, commercial astronaut and pilot. Known in flight by his callsign "Rook" which he was given during fighter jet training, Isaacman has so far logged over 8,000 flight hours. In 2009, he broke the world record for fastest trip around the world in a light jet (he made the trip in 61 hours, 51 minutes and 15 seconds) and is flight-qualified in a number of military jet aircraft. He also financed and flew on two private orbital space missions on a SpaceX Dragon, Inspiration4 and Polaris Dawn, performing the world's first private spacewalk on the latter misison.

Before jumping out of a plane and careening through the air on Saturday as part of this celebratory stunt, Isaacman was actually flying overhead in not one, but two different fighter jets.

First, he flew an F-5, a lightweight supersonic fighter jet, and just a short while later, Isaacman flew a MiG-29, a twin-engine supersonic fighter jet, over the crowd of excited air show attendees. And the fun didn't stop with this skydive, as Isaacman took to the skies once again, flying over the event in fighter jets on Sunday.

This weekend's MAX POWER events are not a one-time-only celebration of aviation and aerospace at NASA. Earlier in the weekend, the agency announced that in 2028, a week-long event called CAPEWEEK will return to the Kennedy Space Center, promising a next-level showcase of air and space innovation and spectacle.

Isaacman and NASA astronauts presented President Donald Trump, who was onhand for the ceremony, with a gold plaque in his honor that will be installed at the Kennedy Space Center's Shuttle Landing Facility runway in time for the CAPEWEEK in 2028.

"What you are seeing today again, imagine March 2028," Isaacman said of the future. "It's going to be 10x bigger. I mean, not just the the fighter aircraft you're seeing, but displays of aerospace-related hardware, rovers, landers. We're going to bring commercial airliners in here ... I would bet on this, the next new Grand Airliner will be announced here."

"That kind of ambition is exactly that you should expect from your space agency," he added. "I promise you, there'll be more to come."
